reference.source: American Academy of Sleep Medicine ICSD-3
clinicalPearls: A circadian rhythm sleep-wake disorder in which the internal clock is not entrained to the 24-hour day, so sleep timing drifts progressively later each day
Patients cycle through periods of good alignment with conventional night-time sleep followed by periods of daytime sleepiness and night-time insomnia
It is most common in people who are totally blind and lack the light input needed to entrain the clock
Sighted cases occur and may relate to weak light exposure, altered clock sensitivity or delayed sleep-wake phase disorder
Diagnosis relies on a prolonged sleep diary, usually with actigraphy, showing the steady daily drift
Timed melatonin, and a melatonin-receptor agonist in some cases, can help entrain the rhythm
reference.pathophysiology: The human circadian pacemaker in the suprachiasmatic nucleus has an intrinsic period slightly longer than 24 hours and normally is reset each day mainly by light. When this entrainment fails, most often because blindness removes photic input to the pacemaker, the sleep-wake rhythm free-runs on its own longer-than-24-hour cycle, drifting out of and back into phase with the environment. Impaired or mistimed light signalling and abnormal melatonin regulation underlie the sighted cases.
additionalInvestigations: Extended sleep diary over several weeks
Actigraphy to document the progressive phase drift
Assessment of visual function and light exposure
Where available, markers of circadian phase such as melatonin timing
Screening for mood disorder that can accompany the misalignment
redFlags: Severe functional or occupational impairment from misalignment
New neurological signs suggesting a broader disorder
Failure to respond to appropriately timed treatment
reference.prognosis: The disorder tends to be chronic, but appropriately timed melatonin or a melatonin-receptor agonist, and light where vision permits, can achieve and maintain entrainment in many patients.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as simple insomnia or delayed sleep-wake phase disorder
Not recognising the high prevalence among totally blind people
Giving melatonin at the wrong circadian time and worsening alignment
Relying on a single night's study rather than longitudinal monitoring
